node.label: Ramsay Cook
node.date_label: “Canadian Centennial Cerebrations” 1967 · The Maple Leaf Forever 1971 · “Regionalism Unmasked” 1983 · The Regenerators 1985 · “Cabbages Not Kings” 1990 · “Identities Are Not Like Hats” 2000
node.description: An English-Canadian historian of nationalism, Quebec and Victorian thought. Attacking a nationalist manifesto in the centennial year, he suggested that 'instead of constantly deploring our lack of identity, we should attempt to understand and explain the regional, ethnic and class identities that we do have. It might just be that it is in these limited identities that “Canadianism” is found' (1967, as quoted by Buckner); Careless made 'limited identities' a programme in 1969. Cook did not make region his unit of analysis: reviewing regional syntheses, he doubted 'the existence of the phenomena we have for so long called regions' and judged that 'as a tool of analysis, “regionalism” is a concept whose time has gone' (1983). The Regenerators (1985) read late Victorian social critics as replacing 'man's salvation' with 'a concern for social salvation', so that Christianity became 'less rather than more relevant' (as quoted by Gauvreau); Michael Gauvreau answered in 1991 that the book rests on 'military metaphors' that recent studies had abandoned, and a 1998 review named Cook, with David Marshall, the strongest advocate of the 'secularization thesis'. His lecture 'Cabbages Not Kings' (1990) proposed an ecological reading of contact in which 'Cabbages, at least as much as kings, led to the transformation of the new world'. In the quarrel over national history he called the debate between 'nationalists' and 'limited identitarians' 'arid' (1993), and in 2000 he argued that identities are 'contingent' and 'multiple rather than single'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Ramsay Cook (1931–2016); Canada and the French-Canadian Question (1966); “Canadian Centennial Cerebrations” (International Journal, 1967); The Maple Leaf Forever: Essays on Nationalism and Politics in Canada (1971); Canada 1896–1921: A Nation Transformed (1974, with Robert Craig Brown); “The Burden of Regionalism” (Acadiensis, 1977); “Regionalism Unmasked” (Acadiensis, 1983); The Regenerators: Social Criticism in Late Victorian English Canada (1985); “Cabbages Not Kings: Towards an Ecological Interpretation of Early Canadian History” (Journal of Canadian Studies, 1990–91); “The New History of Atlantic Canada” (Acadiensis, 1993); “‘Identities Are Not Like Hats’” (Canadian Historical Review, 2000). Readings: Careless (1969); Gaffield (1986); Karr (1989); Gauvreau (1991); Marshall (1993–94); Buckner (2000).
node.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: three of Cook's Acadiensis review essays in full (1977, 1983, 1993), the opening of the 1967 article (OpenAlex text) and the abstract of his 2000 forum piece. The limited-identities sentence (1967) and the 1970 essay reprinted in The Maple Leaf Forever are known through Buckner's (2000) and Karr's (1989) quotations. The Regenerators is unread: its words appear here as quoted by Gauvreau (1991) and Karr, with Gaffield's 1986 review and the book's contents. 'Cabbages Not Kings' was read for the environment drafts on 2026-10-13 and is not re-read here. Canada and the French-Canadian Question is unread. He is not presented as a founder: Buckner says Cook coined 'limited identities' and Careless popularized it, and Cook wrote in 1995 that the phrase was 'usually attributed to Maurice Careless and I have decided that he is welcome to it!' (quoted by Buckner). Contested in period: Gauvreau (1991) on The Regenerators and on limited identities as a frame that marginalized religion; Karr (1989) on his 'anti-national crusade'; Buckner (2000) on the additive idea of identity he attributes to Cook and Careless. Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' (1991–92) is read only in its abstract, which does not name Cook.

proposed_edges.relationship: 'Limited identities': the regional, ethnic and class identities Canadians have, proposed as the place where 'Canadianism' might be found (1967), a phrase Careless made a programme (1969)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cook's own text, 'Canadian Centennial Cerebrations', International Journal 22:4 (1967), pp. 659–663: the opening, read in the OpenAlex text of the article, attacks Canadian Dimension's 'Open Letter to Canadian Nationalists', likens it to Canada First's 1874 manifesto and asks 'Who says Canadian nationalism is difficult to define? Jobs!' (p. 659). The limited-identities sentence was not read on Cook's page; Buckner quotes it (2000, p. 4): 'Perhaps instead of constantly deploring our lack of identity, we should attempt to understand and explain the regional, ethnic and class identities that we do have. It might just be that it is in these limited identities that “Canadianism” is found'. Taken up: Careless (CHR 1969; unread here, quoted by Buckner, p. 4) held that the 'Canadian experience' must be 'discerned and defined' through the 'limited identities of region, culture and class referred to by Professor Cook'. Buckner (p. 5) writes that 'Cook and Careless' embraced the concept partly in response to Quebec separatism, quoting Cook's 1970 essay as reprinted in The Maple Leaf Forever (p. 213): 'Nationalism by nature tends strongly to centralism and uniformity: Canada is by nature federal, sectional and pluralist'; 'historians in Atlantic Canada eagerly espoused the concept of “limited identities”, but their motivations were rather different' (p. 5). In period, Buckner's 1988 abstract (recorded in cdng_buckner_1988, not re-read) calls it 'the catch phrase of the Canadian historical profession in the 1960s' and judges it 'premature to abandon'. Criticism: Reid (1987, opening, recorded in cdng_reid_1987) notes that during the 1980s 'concern has increasingly been expressed that fragmentation has been the result'; Gauvreau (1991, p. 164 n. 10) writes that limited identities 'has underwritten much of the “new social history”', which, like the older national history, 'marginalizes religious history'; Buckner (2000, p. 12) writes 'I think it implied to Cook and Careless' that national identity was the sum of component identities, calls that idea 'nonsensical', and argues that 'All identities are socially constructed'. Influence rather than contribution: Cook named the identities but wrote no regional history, and later questioned region as a unit of analysis (edge 2). The roster row calls him a precursor.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The limited_identities strand names Cook, Careless and Buckner and cites the same 1967, 1969, 1988 and 2000 texts; the evidence fits it exactly.

proposed_edges.relationship: Region questioned as a unit of analysis: regional history's strengths and weaknesses weighed (1977), and regions recast as provinces, 'a concept whose time has gone' (1983)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cook's own review essays in Acadiensis, read in full. 'The Burden of Regionalism' (7:1, Autumn 1977, pp. 110–115), reviewing Bercuson's Canada and the Burden of Unity among other books, notes 'the tendency to see regionalism as a virtue of Canadian life rather than an obstacle to Canadian unity' (p. 110). Bercuson's contributors assume 'that Canadian history is best understood from a regional perspective' (p. 112), but 'neither he nor anyone else in the book attempts to define the term' (p. 114); 'the “regional” approach to Canadian history, and to its discontents, has both strengths and weaknesses. The whole may not be greater than the parts, but it is at least the sum of them' (p. 115). 'Regionalism Unmasked' (13:1, Autumn 1983, pp. 137–142), reviewing L. D. McCann's Heartland and Hinterland (1982): 'I have begun to doubt seriously the existence of the phenomena we have for so long called regions, though regionalism as a rationalization of certain interests may have some reality' (p. 140); McCann's definition of region 'applies at least as well, and perhaps better, to a province as to a region. So why not call a region what it really is — a province' (p. 140); with Cole Harris's chapter, the book 'can really lead to no other conclusion than that, as a tool of analysis, “regionalism” is a concept whose time has gone' (p. 141). He qualifies this: 'Stripped of its rhetoric there remains with the regional approach, especially as practised by historical geographers, a legitimate preoccupation with some profoundly important aspects of our history: class, sex, family, ethnicity, for example' (p. 141), and he calls Wynn's Maritimes chapter 'the finest section of the book' (p. 138). In-period response: Buckner (2000, pp. 8–10) cites both reviews, though he dates the first 1974 and renders 'whose time is gone' where the 1983 page reads 'has gone'. He calls the fragmentation charge 'patently absurd, at least when applied to the Atlantic region' (p. 8) and holds that the Atlantic Provinces 'had legitimate grievances within Confederation' (p. 10), adding that he was 'initially ... as skeptical as Cook' (p. 10). The critique targets the regional framework and heartland–hinterland synthesis, not regional research as such.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The questioning_region strand gathers reassessments of region as a frame (McKay, Friesen and Buckner in 2000). Cook's reviews are earlier statements of the same question, from a centralist direction; reviewers may prefer to add Cook to the strand's person_ids at release.
proposed_edges.roster_row_note: Cook's cdn_regional roster row (precursor) can hold one edge_id; it goes to edge 1, whose influence kind matches the precursor role. This critique is a second arrow to the same entry with a different type.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Laurentian view criticised as regional rather than national, and the national school read as superseded (1977–83)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cook's own words, read in full. 'The Burden of Regionalism' (Acadiensis 7:1, 1977, p. 110): 'The so-called national schools have, in reality, had a rather obviously regional focus. Those who live in the Valley of the Fraser, the Red or the Restigouche can hardly accept the Laurentian view of Canadian history as “national”, unless, of course, they are content to be considered as “colonials” — a point made long ago by W. L. Morton. And the other nationalist themes fare little better.' 'Regionalism Unmasked' (Acadiensis 13:1, 1983, p. 137): 'the so-called “national” approach to the interpretation of the Canadian past has come under a destructive barrage of criticism' (the decade before it is garbled in the text layer); Berger's The Writing of Canadian History (1976) 'might be viewed as a lengthy epitaph on the headstone of the national school's grave'; Morton's 'Clio in Canada' (1946) 'made explicit what had long been implicit in the Innis-Creighton laurentian thesis: the metropolitan-hinterland relationship was not one of equality'. In-period context: Buckner (2000, pp. 4–5) sets limited identities (edge 1) against a post-war consensus of 'liberal nationalists such as A.R.M. Lower and Frank Underhill' and 'conservative nationalists such as Donald Creighton and C.P. Stacey' for whom the nation-state was the frame of reference. Limits: Cook credits the point to Morton; he co-wrote a Centenary Series volume (1974); and by Buckner's account (p. 8) he 'warned regional historians of the danger of ignoring the “national experience”' in 1977 ('The Golden Age of Canadian Historical Writing', Historical Reflections; unread here). The critique is of the Laurentian claim to speak for the nation, not of the staple studies' economics. edge_805 (cdn_regional → cdn_national_tradition, critique) carries the regional historians' version of the argument.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The laurentian strand is Creighton's narrative, the position Cook names ('the Laurentian view', 'the Innis-Creighton laurentian thesis').
proposed_edges.roster_row_note: Not linked (Sol 1.136 finding 2): his cdn_national_tradition row describes the 1974 Centenary volume and 'limited identities', a contribution, not this 1977–83 critique.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Regenerators: late Victorian social criticism read as the replacement of individual by social salvation, and the sacred becoming secular (1985)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The book is unread here: UTP and De Gruyter refused automated access, and the Internet Archive copy is borrow-only. Its contents are recorded in crr_cook_1985, including the closing chapter 'The Sacred Becomes the Secular'. Cook's words are known as quoted in in-period readings. Gauvreau (Acadiensis 1991, pp. 161–162) quotes 'the orthodox Christian preoccupation with man's salvation was gradually replaced by a concern for social salvation' and 'the substitution of theology, the science of religion, with sociology, the science of society' (Regenerators, p. 4); Christianity became 'less rather than more relevant' (p. 6); social conservatism 'went hand in hand with scientific conservatism, and both were founded on religious conservatism' (p. 12); and social regeneration became 'a substitute for the formidable labour of reformulating theological doctrine' (p. 229). Karr (Acadiensis 1989, p. 162) quotes that the book's subjects 'almost never alluded to the cultivation of a national sentiment' (p. 6). Gaffield's review (History: Reviews of New Books 14:5, 1986, p. 144; scanned page read by OCR and checked against the image) summarizes it: 'the call for social salvation emerged from a strong religious commitment but led to increasing secularization', and Cook 'treats religious thinking as an independent factor'. Contested in period. Gauvreau (1991) calls it 'important' but says it 'does not fully resist the temptation to view the 19th-century religious experience in relation to the 20th-century mind-set' (p. 161). He reads it as a '“neo-conservative” appropriation' of Allen's categories (p. 163); 'The appearance of The Regenerators in 1985 marked the beginning of the assault on Allen's position' (p. 163 n. 9). He adds that 'the emerging consensus seems to be away from “military metaphors” of the type employed by Cook' (p. 164). Van Die, he reports, 'ultimately accepts Cook's central thesis of the decline and irrelevance of Protestant religion, but does not agree with the conflict model' (p. 173). Marshall (CCHA Historical Studies 1993–94, web text without page numbers) names 'the secularization thesis outlined by McKillop, Cook, and Marshall' as Gauvreau's target and cites Regenerators pp. 228–32 (n. 6). Laverdure's 1998 review (crr_laverdure_1998, not re-read) says Christie and Gauvreau 'challenge the secularization thesis, most strongly advocated by Ramsay Cook … and David Marshall'. Karr (1989, p. 163 n. 21) finds 'an equally forceful Ontario bias' answering Allen's Western one. The name 'secularization thesis' is the critics', as the strand note says.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The secularization_thesis strand names Cook and Marshall and cites The Regenerators; the social_gospel strand (Allen and Cook) is the alternative, but the in-period debate the evidence records concerns secularization.

proposed_edges.relationship: An ecological interpretation of early Canadian history: contact as the interaction of ecologies, 'cabbages, at least as much as kings' (1990)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Reuses the reading recorded on 2026-10-13 for the environment-family drafts (pe131_extras_cook_1990; canon-evidence-canada.md, text C1). It was not re-read for this entry because Project MUSE refused automated access. Cook's W. L. Morton Lecture (Trent, October 1990; JCS 25:4, 1990–91) starts from Morton's 1946 remark that history 'is concerned with ecology too' (p. 5): 'It is an insight which I would like to try to build upon' (p. 6). He marks a break with the staple historians: 'for this earlier generation of historians the exploitation of the environment was accepted as natural and necessary, even though excesses might be deplored' (pp. 6–7), while 'More recent environmental historians have a different focus. They are no longer much concerned with explaining the impact of the environment on man; it is the impact of man on nature that is at the centre of their work' (p. 7). Following Crosby, 'contact was even more significantly the interaction of different ecologies or environments' (p. 13). His conclusion: 'Cabbages, at least as much as kings, led to the transformation of the new world' (p. 15, as recorded in canon-evidence-canada.md; not in the source's verification note). In-period reading: Gauvreau (Acadiensis 1991, pp. 164–165 n. 12), arguing about Cook's religious history, called the lecture his 'recent “conversion experience” concerning the happy convergence of nature and culture'. Later reading, labelled: Wynn (2004, p. 33, recorded in pe131_extras_wynn_2004) quotes Cook's claim that Canadian historical writing 'has always been concerned with the environment' to describe Canadians who 'seemed to wonder what all the fuss was about'. A contribution, not a founding. edge_913 (harold_a_innis → environment) carries his continuity claim and Forkey's 1998 rejection of it; this edge carries his own ecological reading of contact.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The ecological_exchange strand (organisms, conquest and ecological exchange) is the Crosby line that the lecture applies to contact in New France (p. 13). The environment entry has no Canadian strand; the environment-family notes asked whether to add one.

proposed_edges.relationship: Between 'nationalists' and 'limited identitarians': class, ethnicity and gender as what Canadians share, and identities as contingent and multiple (1993–2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cook's own words. 'The New History of Atlantic Canada' (Acadiensis 23:1, Autumn 1993, pp. 146–152, read in full) came between Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' (1991–92) and Granatstein's book (1998): 'one of the sweet ironies in the arid debate between “nationalists” and “limited identitarians” on historiography is that neither side appears to recognize that class, ethnicity and gender describe what groups of Canadians have in common, while “nationalism” most often provokes divisions — “regionalism”!' (p. 146). He holds that 'for all the emphasis on differences during recent decades, Canadians from all regions and linguistic groups have, in fact, been growing more alike, at least in aspiration if not in reality' (p. 146). His 2000 CHR forum essay (pp. 260–265 per Buckner's n. 15) is read only in its abstract: the 'limited identities' hypothesis 'has played a major role in the flowering of social history whose dominance is now being called into question by proponents of a renewed “national” approach'; the debate ignores 'the easy assumption that identities, limited or national, are essential rather than contingent', and 'it is too often forgotten that identities are multiple rather than single'. Context: Bliss's abstract (1991–92) asks historians to remember 'that their subject, after all, is Canada' and does not name Cook. Buckner (2000) writes that Cook in 1995 called the phrase 'usually attributed to Maurice Careless and I have decided that he is welcome to it!' (p. 8; Canada, Quebec and the Uses of Nationalism, 2nd ed., p. 230, unread here). Buckner then groups Bliss, Granatstein and Owram with Careless's later view that the search for limited identities had 'gone too far' (p. 9). A contribution: Cook is a root of the debate (edge 1) and a respondent who in 1993 placed himself outside both camps.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The reassessments_2000 strand names Cook and cites the 2000 forum; the 1993 essay is an earlier statement of the same position. limited_identities_roots carries 1967 and is covered by edge 1 at cdn_regional.

proposed_edges.relationship: Nationalism as an object of criticism: English-Canadian nationalist intellectuals read from Canada First to the 1960s, against a 'strait-jacket identity' (1967–71)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cook's own text, 1967 (opening read in the OpenAlex text): Canadian Dimension's call for a union of nationalists 'of all parties' is set beside the 1874 call of 'William Foster and his exuberant young friends' (Canada First), and he answers 'Who says Canadian nationalism is difficult to define? Jobs!' (International Journal 22:4, p. 659). Two passages from 1970 are known only through quotation. Karr (Acadiensis 1989, p. 162) quotes Cook (Saturday Night, April 1970): 'Every generation of Canadian nationalist intellectuals ... seems to play the part of Sisyphus. Their permanent task is to push the millstone of Canadian nationalism up a steep mountain, only to find that it rolls back down again to await the labour of the next generation. This means that much of Canadian intellectual history sounds like a broken record'. Buckner (2000, p. 4) quotes the 1970 South Atlantic Quarterly essay, reprinted in The Maple Leaf Forever (1971, pp. 197–214): Canada 'stubbornly refuses to exchange its occasionally anarchic pluralism for a strait-jacket identity. Perhaps it is this heterogeneous pluralism itself that is the Canadian identity'. In-period reading: Karr (1989, p. 162) writes that 'it was Ramsay Cook who did so much to heighten English Canada's understanding of French-Canadian nationalism who led the anti-national crusade', and that 'While it may be easy for many to agree with Cook's belittling of this recurring obsession with national identity, there are problems inherent in extremes on both sides'. His n. 18 adds: 'while Cook is opposed to divisive nationalism, he is a centralist and appears to be searching for a cohesive, positive form of national consensus' (p. 162). Gaffield (1986, p. 143) calls him 'one of Canada's major anglophone “windows” on francophone Québec'. The Maple Leaf Forever and Canada and the French-Canadian Question (1966) are unread here. The Regenerators' place in this field is carried by edge_825.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The empire_and_nation strand names Berger and Cook and cites The Maple Leaf Forever; it treats nationalist thought as an object of study, which is what the quoted passages do.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Not proposed. His Quebec work, Canada and the French-Canadian Question (1966) and the French-Canadian Nationalism anthology (1969), is unread: the Internet Archive copies are borrow-only. His CHA paper 'Some French-Canadian Interpretations of the British Conquest' (Historical Papers 1966; Érudit 10.7202/030653ar) sits behind Érudit's anti-scraping challenge, which was not bypassed. He has no roster row there. The 1993 essay read here notes that Histoire du Québec contemporain made Quebec 'what Michel Brunet always denied: a “normal” society' (p. 147), but that is a remark, not an argument with the normal_society_debate strand. A Quebec evaluation should decide whether English-Canadian readers of Quebec historiography belong in that entry. The Quebec work appears in the description through Karr's and Gaffield's readings.

Canada 1896–1921 (1974, with Brown) and his Dafoe books are political history at content level; he has no roster row there, and the Centenary volume sits in cdn_national_tradition/centenary_series. Content work stays on rosters under the person-entry principle.

His 2000 abstract ties limited identities to 'the flowering of social history', and edge_811 already cites it. Edge 6 at who_killed_debate carries his position; a further arrow to social would repeat it.
The Proper Sphere (1976, with Wendy Mitchinson) is an edited documentary collection in a strand works list; he has no roster row there. No edge.

Careless's person entry is being drafted in parallel (Tier 1). If it is accepted, the limited-identities link between the two entries could be drawn there; edge 1 and Careless's own entry should not both carry the 1969 take-up as the main claim. Left for the coordinator.
His criticism of Canadian nationalism (1967–71) does not engage Anderson, Gellner or the other theorists on that roster in the texts read. No edge.
Gauvreau (1991, p. 163 n. 9) reads The Regenerators as the start of an 'assault on Allen's position'. That is folded into edge 4 rather than given a second arrow to the same entry.

verification.note: Read in the University of Ottawa repository scan (uO Research, hdl 10393/36463; DOI 10.20381/ruor-20743), a two-page image PDF with no text layer, transcribed by OCR. The repository citation gives vol. 14, no. 5 (1986): 143–4; the first scan page carries the printed folio 143 and a handwritten note 'v. 14, No. 5, May/June 1986, pp 143-4'. Quoted: Cook as 'professor of history at York University' and 'one of Canada's major anglophone “windows” on francophone Québec' (p. 143); 'the call for social salvation emerged from a strong religious commitment but led to increasing secularization'; Cook 'treats religious thinking as an independent factor' (p. 144). It also notes that 'readers may wonder about how Cook chose his characters, sources, and quotes' and that the book is limited to Protestant English Canada (p. 144). The quotations were checked against the page images rendered at 200 dpi.

cdng_buckner_2000.note: Re-read for the 1.135 Ramsay Cook entry (UNB PDF, pp. 4–5, 8–10, 12, notes 1–5 and 13–20). Quoted: Cook's 1967 sentence on 'the regional, ethnic and class identities that we do have' and Careless's 'limited identities of region, culture and class referred to by Professor Cook' (p. 4); Cook's 1970 essay, 'a strait-jacket identity' (p. 4) and 'Nationalism by nature tends strongly to centralism and uniformity' (p. 5, quoting The Maple Leaf Forever p. 213); Cook and Careless embraced limited identities partly in response to Quebec separatism; Atlantic historians 'eagerly espoused' it with other motives (p. 5); Cook 'mockingly' recalled being made an honorary Maritimer; fragmentation 'patently absurd, at least when applied to the Atlantic region'; in 1977 Cook 'warned regional historians of the danger of ignoring the “national experience”'; 1983, 'regionalism' 'a concept whose time is gone' (the 1983 page reads 'has gone'); 1995, the phrase 'usually attributed to Maurice Careless and I have decided that he is welcome to it!' (p. 8); Careless 1980 and Bliss, Granatstein and Owram on limited identities having gone too far (p. 9); Atlantic 'legitimate grievances within Confederation' (p. 10); the additive model of identity 'nonsensical'; 'All identities are socially constructed' (p. 12). Note 15 dates 'The Burden of Regionalism' Autumn 1974; the review is of 1977 books and its OJS record is 1977. Note 15 also gives Cook's 2000 CHR essay as 81:2 (June 2000), pp. 260–65.

cic_karr_1989.note: Re-read for the 1.135 Ramsay Cook entry (UNB PDF, pp. 161–163). Quoted: Levitt and Cook 'deepened our understanding of Henri Bourassa' (p. 161, n. 11 citing Canada and the French-Canadian Question under a slipped title); 'it was Ramsay Cook who did so much to heighten English Canada's understanding of French-Canadian nationalism who led the anti-national crusade'; Cook's 1970 'Sisyphus' passage (n. 17: Saturday Night, April 1970, p. 19, and the South Atlantic Quarterly essay); The Regenerators' subjects 'almost never alluded to the cultivation of a national sentiment' (n. 18, Regenerators p. 6); 'problems inherent in extremes on both sides'; n. 18, 'while Cook is opposed to divisive nationalism, he is a centralist' (p. 162); n. 21, 'an equally forceful Ontario bias' (p. 163).

crr_marshall_1993.note: Re-read for the 1.135 Ramsay Cook entry (cchahistory.ca web text, no page numbers). Quoted: 'One of the weaknesses that Gauvreau identifies in the secularization thesis outlined by McKillop, Cook, and Marshall'; Gauvreau's demonstration is 'the foundation for his attack on the secularization thesis and how it has been applied by Cook and McKillop'. Note 2 lists Cook's 'Ambiguous Heritage: Wesley College and the Social Gospel Re-considered' (Manitoba History, Spring 1991) and Gauvreau's 'Beyond the Half-Way House' (Acadiensis 20:2, 1991, pp. 158–77); note 6 cites The Regenerators, pp. 228–32.

cdng_cook_1967.note: Opening re-read for the 1.135 Ramsay Cook entry in the OpenAlex text of the article (W2330026937; OCR-like, with words occasionally dropped). It attacks Canadian Dimension's 'Open Letter to Canadian Nationalists' and its call 'for union sacrée of nationalists of all parties' (the OCR reads 'sacr6e'), sets it beside the 1874 call of 'William Foster and his exuberant young friends', and asks 'Who says Canadian nationalism is difficult to define? Jobs!' (p. 659). The limited-identities sentence is not in the opening text and is still read through Buckner 2000, p. 4.

cdng_cook_2000.note: Abstract re-read for the 1.135 Ramsay Cook entry (OpenAlex W2335830690): 'it is too often forgotten that identities are multiple rather than single. As always, in historical studies, the context is crucial.' Buckner 2000 n. 15 gives CHR 81:2 (June 2000), pp. 260–65; Buckner assumes he is the 'Buchner' referred to on p. 262. The body is unread (Project MUSE captcha; UTP 403).
